chapter: New York 1930s and New Orleans expatriates
title: Larry Shields's clarinet influence
summary: Shields's playing was universally respected and influenced imitators of the Dixieland Band.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Who were the great clarinetists? Favorites and rivals

blocks.x: It was an arrangement for Dixen Land Church. But… Were Shields playing then when you first met him? Yes.

He was playing with the revival of Dixen Land… Mm-hm… …the original Dixen Land Group. In fact, they had just finished at the Paramount Theater or something on stage… …very much playing. He was white-haired then… Mm-hm… But young in face and body, and certainly playing very well. And I will say this, I've never met anybody, any time, any place that didn't respect his clarinet play. At any period, you know, his styles changed. Whether they heard him in person or whether they heard records in their records, no matter what period they came from, they all acknowledged him to be a very great clarinet player. He must have had tremendous influence on a lot of people there as shields.

They had all those different fives, the Memphis Five and the Indiana Five and all, when the Dixieland Band made its impact early in the year. They all seemed to try to play like shields, model themselves on the Dixieland.
Must have been a major influence on the music.
This is not true of everybody else in the original Dixieland Band.
No, I think that, well I think that people look up to him, musicians and fans, more than any other man in that band.

I'm quite sure of that. But I remember when I went to New York, Miff Mole was around, and much respected already, and then there was a guy that they called Little Miff. I can't recall now who he was, but there was another Tramone player that they used to call Little Miff Mole. Little Miff at least.
